title: Size is the wrong question. *Space* is the right one.
subtitle: How to read a ship before you read its brochure.

text: Two ships can measure the same and feel nothing alike.
sub: One carries three times the guests. That single number decides your queues, your tenders, your dinner reservations and your quiet.

points.label: Tender queues
points.value: More guests, more tender groups, and a longer wait for the same small boat.

points.label: Dinner at eight
points.value: Restaurant seats scale slower than cabins. Capacity is the constraint, not the menu.

points.label: Where you berth
points.value: Smaller ships fit alongside quays the largest ships must anchor off.

points.label: Crew attention
points.value: Fewer guests per crew member is the least glamorous luxury and the most reliable.

items.head: Guests at double occupancy
items.body: Not maximum capacity. Ask for both, and note the gap — that gap is your school-holiday sailing.

items.head: Guests per crew member
items.body: Published by most luxury lines. Lower is better, and it shows in the second week, not the first.

items.head: Space ratio
items.body: Tonnage divided by guests. A rough index of elbow room per person; compare it within a class only.

text: Choose the ship for how many people you want at breakfast.
sub: Everything else — the itinerary, the suite, the fare — is easier to fix than a ship that is simply too full for you.

title: Send this to whoever you'd share a cabin with
body: Then tell me the two ships you're weighing up and I'll give you a two-line verdict on which suits you.
